newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions, gov't overcome labor reform spat.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions, gov't overcome labor reform spat.

text.p: Argentine unions and the Peronist government Thursday put aside a spat over President Carlos Menem's labor decrees and agreed to put their heads together to solve the country's employment and economic ills.

"We confirm there is the political will to negotiate a social pact where naturally business leaders will also sit down at the table," CGT labor federation chief Rodolfo Daer told a news conference after the agreement was reached.
Menem's Cabinet Chief Jorge Rodriguez, standing at Daer's side, expressed "the government's satisfaction that dialogue that had been interrupted will now continue."
The CGT led a strike on December 26, its third last year, to protest three decrees signed by Menem forcing through reforms to loosen union control on collective pay talks.
Menem, who faces tough mid-term elections in Congress in October, argues that only the "flexibilization" of labor laws can help the country combat 17.3 percent unemployment.
But the unions fear he means to reduce their power and take away workers' acquired rights.
Labor courts appear to agree: one judge quickly ruled his decrees unconstitutional and another suspended them and then annulled them completely.
Daer, while accepting this week a government invitation to discuss the possibility of resuming dialogue, had urged Menem not to carry out his threat to appeal the rulings.
But Menem insisted to state television Wednesday that the rulings were "clearly political" and Rodriguez told the news conference the appeal had been lodged earlier Thursday.
"We see this as a bad step," responded Daer.

Analysts say the decrees, which would let firms bypass national unions in wage talks and negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis -- were really meant as a slap in the face to unions, and the main body of the reforms would still have to go through Congress.
Rodriguez took a conciliatory tone, saying "The labor issues in those decrees are also going to be resolved by the dialogue we are establishing from today with the CGT."
And Interior Minister Carlos Corach, attending the talks at CGT headquarters, said Menem had instructed them "there must be no suspicion, no mistrust."
The CGT wants the talks to go beyond employment and include broad economic issues such as taxes and small enterprises.

But Rodriguez made it clear the government was not about to jettison economic policy at the CGT's behest. "There is no change of direction, the CGT will just contribute such as in the fight against tax evasion," said Rodriguez.
